## 1. Episode I – The Phantom Menace
**Plot:** The Jedi Qui-Gon Jinn and his Padawan Obi-Wan Kenobi are sent to resolve a trade blockade of Naboo. They rescue Queen Amidala, crash on Tatooine, and find a 9-year-old slave, Anakin Skywalker, who is abnormally strong in the Force. Qui-Gon dies fighting Darth Maul; Obi-Wan takes Anakin as his apprentice.
**Quote:** *"Fear is the path to the dark side."* / *"Now this is podracing!"*
**Impact:** The prequels were the biggest hype-to-backlash swing in film history, but a generation that grew up with them now loves them unironically — a huge, loyal, meme-native audience. Darth Maul's double-bladed lightsaber instantly became an iconic toy.
**Hook:** Podracing = a perfect Lego build-and-race minigame/limited event. Maul's double saber is a premium unlockable.

## 2. Episode II – Attack of the Clones
**Plot:** Ten years later. Anakin, now Obi-Wan's surly Padawan, is assigned to protect Senator Padmé Amidala and falls for her. Obi-Wan uncovers a secret clone army and a Separatist droid army; the film ends with the Clone Wars igniting at the Battle of Geonosis.
**Quote:** *"I don't like sand."* (one of the most-memed lines in the franchise)
**Impact:** Established the "army vs. army" visual language — clone troopers vs. battle droids — which is the single most toy-friendly conflict in the saga (endless army-building).

**Plot:** Anakin, manipulated by Chancellor Palpatine, turns on the Jedi to save Padmé from a vision of her death. Order 66 wipes out the Jedi; Anakin is maimed and becomes Darth Vader; Padmé dies giving birth to Luke and Leia; the Republic becomes the Empire.
**Quote:** *"You were my brother, Anakin! I loved you!"* / Vader's *"Noooo!"*
**Impact:** The tragic pivot of the whole saga; Order 66 is a cultural shorthand for betrayal and is endlessly referenced. It's the emotional anchor that makes Vader sympathetic.
**Hook:** A "Order 66" survival event (play as a hunted Jedi) is an obvious high-drama limited-time mode.

## 4. Solo: A Star Wars Story
**Plot:** Origin of Han Solo: a street thief who joins an Imperial academy, deserts, meets Chewbacca and Lando, wins the Millennium Falcon in a card game, and makes the Kessel Run.
**Quote:** *"I have a good feeling about this."* (deliberate inversion of Han's famous line)
**Impact:** Commercially the franchise's cautionary tale (production turmoil, underperformance) — proof that Star Wars fans reward *recognizable* iconography over new-cast backstory.
**Hook:** The Falcon + Kessel Run = a great heist/time-trial event template.

## 5. Rogue One: A Star Wars Story
**Plot:** A team of rebels steals the Death Star plans, and all of them die getting the data out. The film ends minutes before A New Hope begins.
**Quote:** *"Rebellions are built on hope."*
**Impact:** Widely considered the best of the modern films; proved Star Wars works as a gritty war/heist genre piece. The Vader hallway scene is one of the most-shared sequences in the franchise.
**Hook:** Co-op heist mission with a "sacrifice" ending — strong seasonal story event.

## 6. Episode IV – A New Hope
**Plot:** Farm boy Luke Skywalker joins Obi-Wan, smuggler Han Solo, and Princess Leia to rescue her and destroy the Death Star. Obi-Wan dies dueling Vader; Luke uses the Force to make the impossible shot.
**Quote:** *"May the Force be with you."*
**Impact:** The origin point of modern blockbuster franchise culture, ILM-era VFX, and merchandising-as-industry. This is the imagery everyone on earth recognizes in one frame.
**Hook:** Your "tutorial + flagship" content. This is the box art.

## 7. Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back
**Plot:** The Empire routs the Rebels on Hoth; Luke trains with Yoda on Dagobah; Han is frozen in carbonite and taken by Boba Fett; Luke duels Vader and loses a hand — and learns Vader is his father.
**Quote:** *"No, I am your father."* (the most quoted plot twist in cinema)
**Impact:** The template for the "dark second act" in franchise storytelling, and the reason sequels are allowed to end on a downbeat. Boba Fett became a fan-favorite from almost no screen time.
**Hook:** "Escalation" season — the midpoint turn where you reveal the big twist/boss.

## 8. Episode VI – Return of the Jedi
**Plot:** Luke surrenders to Vader to try to redeem him; the Rebels assault the second Death Star with the Ewoks on Endor; Vader throws Palpatine down a reactor shaft to save his son and dies redeemed.
**Quote:** *"It's a trap!"*
**Impact:** Ewoks are the franchise's original "too cute / too commercial" controversy — and a direct ancestor of the Lego-game tone. The redemption arc is the saga's emotional payoff.
**Hook:** Redemption finale + Ewok/tribal comedic content; "It's a trap!" is a ready-made event title.

*Then:* **The Mandalorian** (post-Return of the Jedi) — a bounty hunter protects a Force-sensitive child. *"This is the way."* Culturally it re-energized the brand and made "Baby Yoda" a global merchandising phenomenon — proof that one adorable character can carry a whole product line.

## 9. Episode VII – The Force Awakens
**Plot:** 30 years later, the First Order rises. Scavenger Rey, defector stormtrooper Finn, and pilot Poe Dameron help find Luke, who has vanished.
**Quote:** *"Chewie, we're home."* (the marketing line that sold the whole film)
**Impact:** Deliberately a nostalgia remake of A New Hope; record-breaking box office, and it reset the franchise around a new trio and a female lead.
**Hook:** "Return of the classic" relaunch event — good pattern for your own seasonal resets.

## 10. Episode VIII – The Last Jedi
**Plot:** Rey trains with a bitter Luke; the Resistance fleet is destroyed in slow pursuit; Snoke is killed by Kylo Ren; Luke dies projecting himself across the galaxy to save the Resistance.
**Quote:** *"This is not going to go the way you think."*
**Impact:** The most divisive film in the franchise — a real lesson that subverting fan expectations can fracture a community. Worth studying for how *not* to break player trust in live-ops.
**Hook:** Cautionary design reference for community sentiment.

## 11. Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker
**Plot:** Palpatine returns; Rey is revealed as his granddaughter; she and a redeemed Ben Solo defeat him; Ben dies; Rey takes the Skywalker name.
**Quote:** *"Somehow, Palpatine returned."* (now shorthand for a contrived comeback)
**Impact:** Widely criticized for retconning the previous film — the franchise's clearest case study that reactive, fan-panic-driven course correction reads as incoherent. Directly relevant if you plan live "retcon" patches.
**Hook:** Design lesson: never let loud feedback override your narrative spine.

---

**The five things that matter most for your game**

1. **The Force** — the one abstract idea everyone knows; make it a resource/meter, light vs. dark as a visible progression axis.
2. **Lightsabers + the binary "Light Side / Dark Side"** — clean, readable, instantly marketable.
3. **The Empire vs. Rebels / clones vs. droids** — two-faction army building is the most toy-compatible structure Star Wars offers (and it's exactly Lego's strength).
4. **Iconic props and characters** (Falcon, Death Star, Vader, R2-D2, Baby Yoda) — recognizability beats novelty in this IP; reveal them as the payoff of events, not the premise.
5. **Quotes as event names** — "It's a trap!", "May the Force be with you", "This is the way" are free, pre-loaded branding for time-limited events and seasonal taglines.

And the meta-lesson from the sequels: fans bond to *specific* iconography and *specific* characters. Subvert gameplay, not their emotional anchors.

**A couple of things I do remember about your running:**

*(One gap: I don't have the exact model name of your current pair on file — if you tell me, I can search for it and for the closest current equivalent.)*

**Why the April timing helps**

Outlet pricing follows a fairly predictable cycle. April is when spring models land at full price and last year's version gets pushed to clearance — which is likely exactly why you scored 20% off. That same cycle repeats around late May/early June (Memorial Day → Father's Day sales), so you're looking at a decent window right now.

**Where to look for the same model**

1. **Nike Outlet site / Nike Clearance** — filter by your model name; older colorways of still-current models often sit at 30–40% off.
2. **Nike Factory Stores** — call ahead and ask if they have your model in your size; stock at outlets is per-store and phone checks save a wasted trip.
3. **6pm, Nordstrom Rack, Saks Off 5th, Running Warehouse** — these are the usual graveyards for previous-season Nike runners, often deeper discounts than Nike's own outlet.
4. **Amazon / Zappos** — worth a price check, but watch for third-party sellers and mismatched sizes.

**If your exact model is gone**

Nike almost always keeps a model in the line-up for 2–3 generations, so the direct successor is the safest "same fit" bet (Pegasus → Pegasus, Structure → Structure, Vomero → Vomero, etc.). The midsole and last usually change only slightly between consecutive versions — much less than jumping to a different Nike line.

**Two practical tips**
- Sizes tend to disappear first at outlets; if you find your model, don't sit on it.
- Don't trust the "% off" tag alone — outlet "compare at" prices are sometimes inflated. Check the model's street price on Running Warehouse or Amazon before you commit.

answer:
Happy to pick this up — and glad the tour stuck with you. A few thoughts:

**On the "perspective shift" you described:** that's a very common turning point. Once you start reading sculpture as *process + intent* rather than just form, works that seemed opaque often become legible. A useful habit: for each piece, ask what the material choice is doing (why plastic bottles rather than bronze?), and what labor is hidden in the object.

**Sustainable-practice artists worth your time, beyond the plastic-bottle thread:**
- **Aurora Robson** — cut-and-assembled plastic debris into hanging, organic forms; also founded Project Vortex, a network of artists working with plastic.
- **El Anatsui** — monumental "tapestries" from discarded bottle caps and aluminum seals; sustainability via repurposing and craft labor.
- **Studio Swine (Azusa Murakami & Alexander Groves)** — design-art projects like *Sea Chair*, made from plastic recovered from the ocean.
- **John Sabraw** — paints with pigment reclaimed from acid mine drainage.
- **Olafur Eliasson** — large-scale installations engaging climate, water, and light (more experiential than material-reuse, but thematically adjacent).
- **Agnes Denes** — early land art (*Wheatfield – A Confrontation*), foundational for eco-conscious practice.

**For the City Gallery's sustainable-art exhibition:** go in with two questions — (1) is the sustainability in the *material*, the *process*, or the *message*? and (2) does the work address the energy/carbon cost of making and shipping large sculptures? Institutions rarely volunteer the second.

**One gentle caveat:** in my earlier reply I listed some exhibitions with dated runs (2023 windows) and a couple of gallery/artist pairings. Treat those as starting points rather than verified facts — check each institution's site before planning, and note that a few of those attributions are loose.

When you attend the artist talk, ask the artist what they *rejected* while making the piece — the discarded options usually reveal more than the finished object.
